narrative:
The model estimated your chance of failing at 15.0%. That is a low risk—roughly one chance in seven—not a certain failure. If you are being required to take remedial courses, treat this as a precaution based on a nonzero risk estimate rather than a confident forecast that you will fail.

The strongest influences on the estimate actually leaned toward passing. First, your record of past class failures is zero, matching the passing-group average, which is protective. Second, you want to pursue higher education; all students in the passing group also said yes, so this also pushes toward passing. Third, your free time after school is low; compared with passers, who more often report medium or high free time, this factor also leaned toward passing in the model’s assessment. These leading factors make failure look less likely, not more.

The remaining risk appears to come from smaller factors, such as eight absences versus an average of about 3.8, weekly study time under two hours, and a 30–60 minute commute. To improve, keep attendance consistent, build a regular study routine, and use school or family support early. Continue planning for higher education, since that protective intention is a positive signal.
